#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Open one review tab per case, with the before and after diagram side by side
#
# Usage:
#   scripts/viz-review-panes.sh --round 02 [--baseline 01] [--case <case>]
#                              [--bin /abs/rataflow-view] [--view N]
#
# Each tab gets two panes at natural zoom: the baseline round (left, "before")
# and the evaluated round (right, "after"). --view picks which view pair to
# show; panes.json records every available view so another pair can be opened
# later. Panes stay open for the human: this script closes nothing.
set -euo pipefail

die() { printf 'viz-review-panes: %s\n' "$*" >&2; exit 1; }

round='' baseline='01' only_case='' bin='' view=1 repo=$(pwd)
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --round) round=${2:?}; shift 2 ;;
    --baseline) baseline=${2:?}; shift 2 ;;
    --case) only_case=${2:?}; shift 2 ;;
    --bin) bin=${2:?}; shift 2 ;;
    --view) view=${2:?}; shift 2 ;;
    --repo) repo=${2:?}; shift 2 ;;
    -h|--help) sed -n '2,15p' "$0"; exit 0 ;;
    *) die "unknown argument: $1" ;;
  esac
done
[ -n "$round" ] || die "--round is required"
[ "${HERDR_ENV:-}" = 1 ] || die "HERDR_ENV is not 1; review panes need Herdr"
command -v herdr >/dev/null || die "herdr is not on PATH"
command -v jq >/dev/null || die "jq is not on PATH"

round_dir="$repo/docs/visualize-eval/rounds/$round"
base_dir="$repo/docs/visualize-eval/rounds/$baseline"
[ -f "$round_dir/config.json" ] || die "no config.json in $round_dir"
[ -d "$base_dir" ] || die "no baseline round directory: $base_dir"
if [ -z "$bin" ]; then
  bin=$(jq -r '.binary_path // empty' "$round_dir/config.json")
fi
[ -n "$bin" ] || die "no --bin and no binary_path in config.json"
case "$bin" in /*) ;; *) die "--bin must be absolute, got: $bin" ;; esac
[ -x "$bin" ] || die "binary not executable: $bin"

out_dir="$round_dir/human-review"
mkdir -p "$out_dir"
table='[]'

collect_specs() { # collect_specs <dir> -> newline list of final specs, version sorted
  find "$1" -maxdepth 1 -name 'v*.json' 2>/dev/null | sort -V
}

view_of() { # view_of <list-index> <dir> -> the Nth spec, empty when absent
  local wanted=$1 dir=$2 index=0 path
  while IFS= read -r path; do
    if [ "$index" -eq "$((wanted - 1))" ]; then printf '%s' "$path"; return 0; fi
    index=$((index + 1))
  done < <(collect_specs "$dir")
  return 1
}

cases=$(jq -r '.cases[]' "$round_dir/config.json")
for case_id in $cases; do
  if [ -n "$only_case" ] && [ "$case_id" != "$only_case" ]; then
    continue
  fi
  after_dir="$round_dir/$case_id"
  before_dir="$base_dir/$case_id"
  after_spec=$(view_of "$view" "$after_dir" || true)
  before_spec=$(view_of "$view" "$before_dir" || true)
  [ -n "$after_spec" ] || { printf 'skip %s (no view %s after)\n' "$case_id" "$view" >&2; continue; }

  created=$(herdr tab create --label "r$round $case_id v$view" --cwd "$repo" --no-focus)
  tab=$(jq -r '.result.tab.tab_id // empty' <<<"$created")
  root=$(jq -r '.result.root_pane.pane_id // empty' <<<"$created")
  [ -n "$tab" ] && [ -n "$root" ] || die "could not create a tab for $case_id: $created"

  # Left: before. Right: after. Both at natural 100% zoom.
  if [ -n "$before_spec" ]; then
    herdr pane run "$root" "$bin" "$before_spec" >/dev/null
    herdr pane rename "$root" "before v$view" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
  else
    herdr pane run "$root" "printf 'no baseline view %s for %s\n'" "$view" "$case_id" >/dev/null || true
  fi
  after_pane=$(herdr pane split "$root" --direction right --ratio 0.5 --cwd "$repo" --no-focus \
    | jq -r '.result.pane.pane_id // empty')
  [ -n "$after_pane" ] || die "could not split a pane for $case_id"
  herdr pane run "$after_pane" "$bin" "$after_spec" >/dev/null
  herdr pane rename "$after_pane" "after v$view" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true

  before_all=$(collect_specs "$before_dir" | jq -R . | jq -s .)
  after_all=$(collect_specs "$after_dir" | jq -R . | jq -s .)
  entry=$(jq -n --arg case "$case_id" --arg tab "$tab" --argjson view "$view" \
    --arg before "$before_spec" --arg after "$after_spec" \
    --arg bpanes "$root" --arg apanes "$after_pane" \
    --argjson before_all "$before_all" --argjson after_all "$after_all" \
    '{case: $case, tab_id: $tab, view: $view,
      before_spec: (if $before == "" then null else $before end), after_spec: $after,
      before_view_count: ($before_all | length), after_view_count: ($after_all | length),
      before_specs: $before_all, after_specs: $after_all,
      pane_ids: {before: $bpanes, after: $apanes}}')
  table=$(jq -c --argjson e "$entry" '. + [$e]' <<<"$table")
  printf 'opened %-24s tab=%s before=%s after=%s\n' \
    "$case_id" "$tab" "$(basename "${before_spec:-none}")" "$(basename "$after_spec")"
done

jq -n --arg round "$round" --arg baseline "$baseline" --arg bin "$bin" \
  --argjson cases "$table" --arg opened "$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)" \
  '{round: $round, baseline: $baseline, binary: $bin, opened_at: $opened,
    note: "Panes stay open for human review. Left pane is the baseline round, right pane is the evaluated round.",
    cases: $cases}' > "$out_dir/panes.json"

printf '\nreview tabs are open. Close one with: herdr tab close <tab-id>\n'
printf 'manifest: %s\n' "$out_dir/panes.json"

edits.newText:
collect_specs() { # collect_specs <case-dir> -> final spec paths, view order preserved
  # generation.json is the authority on which spec is final and in what order.
  # Its paths are inconsistent across workers (repo-relative, case-relative,
  # round-relative), so resolve each against all three bases.
  local case_dir=$1 base repo_root parent spec candidate
  repo_root=$repo
  parent=$(dirname "$case_dir")
  if [ -f "$case_dir/generation.json" ]; then
    while IFS= read -r spec; do
      [ -n "$spec" ] || continue
      for base in "$repo_root" "$case_dir" "$parent"; do
        candidate="$base/$spec"
        if [ -f "$candidate" ]; then printf '%s\n' "$candidate"; break; fi
      done
    done < <(jq -r '.views[]? | .spec // .spec_path // empty' "$case_dir/generation.json" 2>/dev/null)
    return 0
  fi
  # Fallback for a case without generation.json: scan the usual spec homes.
  local dir
  for dir in "$case_dir/spec" "$case_dir/specs"; do
    [ -d "$dir" ] || continue
    find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name '*.json' 2>/dev/null \
      ! -name '*.split.json' ! -name '*reference*' | sort -V
  done
}
edits.oldText:
collect_specs() { # collect_specs <dir> -> newline list of final specs, version sorted
  # Rounds store final specs differently: baseline `spec/view1.json`, evaluated
  # `v1.json` at the top level or `specs/v1.json`. Attempt files are excluded.
  local dir=$1 sub path
  for sub in spec specs; do
    path="$dir/$sub"
    if [ -d "$path" ]; then
      { find "$path" -maxdepth 1 -name 'view[0-9]*.json' 2>/dev/null
        find "$path" -maxdepth 1 -name 'v[0-9].json' 2>/dev/null
        find "$path" -maxdepth 1 -name 'v[0-9][0-9].json' 2>/dev/null
      } | sort -u -V
      return 0
    fi
  done
  { find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name 'v[0-9].json' 2>/dev/null
    find "$dir" -maxdepth 1 -name 'v[0-9][0-9].json' 2>/dev/null
  } | sort -u -V
}

Implement three renderer changes in the local rataflow crate in `/Users/aviral/.herdr/worktrees/dotfiles/fix-visualize-skill`. Read the existing code first (`rataflow/src/{lib.rs,router.rs,flow_edge.rs,main.rs}`, tests in `rataflow/tests/render.rs`). You own ONLY:

- `rataflow/src/lib.rs`
- `rataflow/src/router.rs`
- `rataflow/src/flow_edge.rs`
- `rataflow/src/main.rs`
- `rataflow/tests/render.rs`
- `rataflow/examples/*.json`

Do NOT edit `rataflow/Cargo.toml` (no new dependencies), `docs/**`, `scripts/**`, `agents/**`, or `AGENTS.md`. Another agent edits those at the same time.

Baseline state: 58 tests pass, Clippy is clean. Preserve every current test unless a requirement below contradicts it; if one must change, say exactly which and why.

## Requirement 1 — synchronized dots (the important one)

Today an edge's dot speed is cells-per-step, so a long route finishes long after a short one. The new default: **every animated route starts at the same instant and reaches its arrowhead at the same instant**, whatever its length.

- New optional edge field `duration_ms` (positive integer, default `2000`). Reject `0`, negatives and non-integers with a message naming the field.
- `flow: true` on an edge keeps meaning "animate this route". Timing now comes from `duration_ms`, not from route length.
- `flow: <positive number>` stays supported as an explicit legacy speed override (cells per 100 ms step) for an edge that should NOT be synchronized. Keep it working and say in the report that it is the documented escape hatch.
- Dot position must be computed from progress, not from a modulo cycle over cells: at step `i` of `duration_ms / 100` steps the dot sits at index `round(i * (n - 1) / steps)` where `n` is the number of drawable route cells. So it is at the first cell on step 0 and at the last cell (the arrowhead cell) on the final step, then wraps.
- **The dot must start at the actual start of the arrow**: the first cell drawn after the source port (the source stem), including when the route leaves the source sideways or wraps around a box. It must never start mid-route, on the source border, or after an initial blank cell.
- A route whose drawable span is too short to show motion (fewer than 3 dot cells) must be reported, not silently animated ambiguously. Add it to the report and a `--check` line.

## Requirement 2 — minimize crossings while routing

The user wants fewer overlaps, without hurting logical order. Layer order stays exactly as the spec declares it: never reorder `layers` or the source's grouping to reduce crossings.

- Route cost must penalize crossing an already-routed perpendicular route (a bridge) more than a detour of a couple of cells, so A* prefers a slightly longer corridor over a crossing where one exists.
- Assign ports on each node side in the order of the far endpoint's position (sorted along the crossing axis), so fans leave in an order that does not braid.
- Keep every existing guarantee: no shared runs, no crossing at a bend, no bridge on a junction, dots never on corners/bridges/junctions/arrowheads.
- Add `crossings` to `Report`: the number of bridge cells drawn (an independent crossing costs 1). Print it in `--check` as its own line `crossings: <n>`.

## Requirement 3 — `--check` lines

Keep the existing lines and add exactly these:

```
crossings: <n>
dots: <n> single-dot routes, <n> periodic routes, <n> violations, <n> synchronized at <ms>ms
origins: <n>/<n> routes start at their arrow origin
```

- `synchronized at <ms>ms` is the shared default duration actually used.
- `origins` must be a real check: count routes whose first dot cell is the first drawn cell adjacent to the source port. A route that fails is also a `violations` increment.
- Keep `labels:`, `groups:`, `trunks:`, `viewport:` unchanged in format.

## Tests to add

1. Two animated routes of very different lengths (one about 5 cells, one about 25) both put their dot on the arrowhead cell at the default duration's final step — synchronized arrival — while their intermediate steps differ.
2. On step 0 every animated route's dot is on the first drawn cell after the source port, for routes leaving down, sideways, and around a box.
3. `duration_ms: 600` makes a route complete in 6 steps; a legacy `flow: 0.5` route is explicitly not synchronized.
4. A too-short route (< 3 dot cells) is reported and does not count as a valid animated route.
5. A layout where a 2-cell detour avoids a crossing chooses the detour, and `crossings` counts what remains.
6. Existing guarantees still hold: no shared runs, no dot on corner/bridge/junction/arrowhead, trunk junctions intact, labels off routes.

## Verify before reporting

```sh
cargo test --offline --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml
cargo clippy --offline --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo build --offline --locked --release --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml
```

## Report back

1. Final schema for animation (`flow`, `duration_ms`) and what each means.
2. How dot index is computed, in one paragraph, and how you guarantee the origin cell.
3. What the crossing-aware cost function charges for a crossing, a bend, and a detour cell.
4. The exact new `--check` output from a real spec, plus the crossings count before/after your change on `rataflow/examples/trunk.json` and on whatever spec you use for the crossing test.
5. Test counts and any test you had to change.
6. Anything you could not satisfy, and why. Do not weaken a test to make it pass.

## What I recorded and changed

- **Your feedback** is now verbatim in `rounds/02/human-review/feedback.md`: synchronized arrival, dot at the arrow origin, fewer overlaps by layout, and "objectively better" as the round verdict.

- **Candidate skill 04** (`proposals/04/SKILL.md`): a motion section with the three rules, `duration_ms` in the schema, crossing guidance, and evidence instructions that require a full 21-frame cycle.
- **Harness:** `viz-validate.py` now rejects a sample without `origins: N/N`, `synchronized at <ms>ms`, or `crossings: N`. Round 02's scripts are snapshotted under `rounds/02/harness/` so that round stays replayable.

## Renderer work in flight

A worker is implementing: progress-based dot timing on a shared 2000 ms duration with `duration_ms` override; dot start on the first drawn cell after the source port; crossing-penalised A* plus port ordering by far-endpoint position; and the new `crossings:` / `origins:` check lines. 58 existing tests must keep passing.

args.content:
# Round 03 decision

## Outcome

**0/8 green. 22 pass / 22 fail / 8 blocked of 52 applicable categories.
7 critical, 28 high, 16 medium findings.** Every case fails; the round is
nevertheless a large qualitative move, and the failures are now precise,
root-caused, and fixable. Frozen inputs: skill `cf796bcdc527…`, binary
`b242b6a28e2e…` (`/tmp/visualize-eval/round-03/bin/rataflow-view`), rubric
revision 4 `5519fd84f6b7…` (motion + crossing rules; reviewer identity
corrected mid-round before any result existed), dataset unchanged from
rounds 01–02. Models: DeepSeek (fireworks) generated, Sol judged; never
shared.

## Verdict matrix (P/F/B, — = source-backed N/A)

| Case | Semantic | Arrows | Fit | Groups | Borders | Workflow | Animation | Overall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| pipeline | P | F | P | P | P | F | F | FAIL |
| network | F | F | F | P | P | B | F | FAIL |
| homelab-nic-trace | F | P | F | P | P | B | — | FAIL |
| server-nic-layout | F | F | F | P | P | B | — | FAIL |
| datacenter-redundancy | P | P | F | P | P | B | **P** | FAIL |
| modal-machine-manager | F | F | F | P | P | B | F | FAIL |
| modal-runtime | F | P | B | P | P | B | — | FAIL |
| gb300-rack-software | F | F | B | F | P | F | — | FAIL |

## Movement against round 02 (1/8 green; 35/13/3 of 51; 10C/14H/2M)

- **Held or improved:** borders 8/8 both rounds; groups 7/8 (gb300's Fabric
  Manager placement is the one failure); datacenter edges 28/28 pass and its
  explicit no-dots request now passes animation in static form — the round-02
  critical violation is closed; `boot.ipxe + S3 args` survives in
  machine-manager (round-02 loss recovered); zero skipped labels across all
  20 views; every reported crossing count now exists.
- **Regressed by design:** the strengthened rubric converted two renderer
  design choices into failures — dot spans skip corner glyphs (frame-0 dots
  one cell downstream: pipeline 6/6, network 7/7, mm 20/20) and the arrowhead
  glyph absorbs the arriving dot (no visible arrival anywhere animated).
  Arrows fell 7P→3P, animation 1B/2F→1P/3F. These are real defects against
  the human-requested rules, not rubric noise.
- **Regressed by enforcement:** workflow evidence fell 6P/2B→0P/6B/2F.
  Judges now uniformly block on the missing independent live-pane rectangle
  (`pane_cols: null` outside the focused tab) and missing probe/cleanup
  provenance. Harness gap, not a rendering gap.
- **Newly exposed:** avoidable crossings judged present in four cases
  (network v2, datacenter v2/v3 hairpins, server v3, mm v4) — the
  crossing-aware router still leaves removable crossings; server's trunk
  reversed three member→gateway relations; homelab traded a required
  `claimed` qualifier for a crossing (forbidden trade, honestly recorded);
  gb300's workflow records contained a false repetition claim; mm's
  full-frame dumps rendered at 80×24.

## Root causes, ranked

1. **Renderer motion design** (blocks 3 animated cases): origin cell and
   arrival visibility. Fix: dot span starts at the first drawn glyph (corner
   or not); arrival frame must show the dot at the arrowhead.
2. **Harness evidence** (blocks 6 cases' workflow): pane rectangle from owned
   pane id, mandatory probe/cleanup/rejected-check logs, target-size frame 0,
   no hardcoded geometry, machine-checkable workflow claims.
3. **Skill gates** (semantic losses): qualifiers and identifiers as required
   coverage rows; trunk direction validated against source relations;
   claims-vs-captures gate (every motion claim cites frame + coordinates);
   port-ordering before accepting crossings.
4. **Router quality** (fit losses): hairpin-detour elimination; single
   split-point trunk (gb300 critical).

## Stop-rule assessment

Continue to round 04. This was candidate revision 2 of the allowed sequence;
it produced useful improvement (borders, groups, datacenter edges, no-dots,
boot.ipxe, crossing reporting), so the no-improvement stop rule does not
apply. All remaining blockers are concrete and fixable; none is an
unsupported capability.

## Round-04 work list

1. Renderer: origin-cell dot spans; visible synchronized arrival; hairpin
   detour elimination; single split-point trunk; dashed style through bends;
   reconcile visible vs counted crossings.
2. Harness: pane rectangle from owned pane id; mandatory rejected-draft raw
   records and cleanup/probe logs; target-size (77×47) direct frame dumps;
   forbid hardcoded geometry; machine-check workflow-record claims against
   spec manifests.
3. Skill: qualifier/identifier coverage gate; trunk direction check;
   claims-vs-captures citations; port-ordering as the first crossing move;
   attempts budget counts every `--check` probe.

Manual human review of round 02 vs round 03 is the blocking next stage;
revision work starts only after feedback is recorded in
`rounds/03/human-review/feedback.md`.

Baseline: 73 tests pass, Clippy clean. Preserve every current test unless a requirement contradicts it; report exactly which tests changed and why. Do not weaken any test.

## Requirement 1 — two motion modes, constant by default

The human reversed the round-03 default. New per-edge field `timing`: `"constant"` (default) or `"same-arrival"`.

- `flow: true` → animate at a **constant shared speed** (the default rate). Pick the default rate to match the legacy periodic feel (check git history / the original crate default; around 0.5 cells per 100 ms step). Document it in `USAGE`.
- `flow: <positive number>` → constant speed at that cells-per-100ms rate (legacy override, unchanged).
- `timing: "same-arrival"` (requires `flow: true`, rejected with numeric `flow`) → the round-03 synchronized behavior: every animated route leaves at t=0 and its dot reaches the arrowhead at `duration_ms` (default 2000). Keep the progress-based index math.
- `duration_ms` is valid ONLY with `timing: "same-arrival"`. Reject it with constant timing or numeric `flow` with a message naming the field. (This intentionally breaks round-03 semantics where `duration_ms` alone animated a route — document that break.)
- `--check` dots line becomes: `dots: <n> single-dot routes, <n> periodic routes, <n> violations, <n> constant at <rate>c/step, <n> same-arrival at <ms>ms` — keep the existing prefix so old parsers still match the head of the line.

## Requirement 2 — dot origin at the first drawn glyph

The dot span must START at the first drawn cell after the source port **including when that cell is a corner glyph** (round 03 skipped corners, so tb routes with side ports started one cell late — judges counted 6/6, 7/7, 20/20 origin violations across cases). Mid-route corners may still be skipped for legibility, but the span's first cell is always the first drawn cell. Keep `origins: N/N routes start at their arrow origin` as a real check that now also verifies corner-first routes.

## Requirement 3 — visible arrival in same-arrival mode

Round 03 painted the arrowhead last, absorbing the arriving dot, so no capture could prove simultaneous arrival. In same-arrival mode the final step must show the dot **visibly at the arrowhead**: pick a legible design (for example a composite dot-on-head glyph, or the dot drawn touching the head cell) so one frame shows every route's dot at its own arrowhead at the same instant. Constant mode keeps the periodic cycle that never rests on the head cell.

## Requirement 4 — route economy

Judges found avoidable hairpin detours (datacenter v2/v3, server v3, machine-manager v4) and the human saw "redundant looping". Add:

- A per-route detour measure: route length versus a shortest-obstacle-safe reference (A* length with bridges disallowed, or a tight lower bound you can compute cheaply). `--check` gains `routes: <n>/<m> near-minimal, <k> detours` plus one warning line per detour route (name from→to, length, reference).
- A shortening pass that removes loops and hairpins while preserving every hard guarantee: separate ports and stems, reserved cells, crossings only through bridges, no shared runs, dots/junction rules, label placement. Run it after routing; report how many routes it shortened.
- Demonstrate on the repo examples and on a two-tier fan spec you write: the datacenter-style hairpin (up-fan and down-fan in one corridor band) must shorten or the detour must be provably forced.

## Requirement 5 — single split-point trunk

gb300's OOB bus must show ONE junction where the corridor splits into all spurs (the source demands a single three-way split; round 03 drew one junction per branch plus a terminating drop). Change trunk routing: corridor from `from` to one junction cell, then parallel spurs from that junction to each branch (the `to` destination may be one spur or the corridor end). One junction glyph total per trunk. Dots never on the junction.

## Requirement 6 — dashed style through bends

A dashed edge must read as dashed along its whole route, bends included — round 03 rendered solid curved bends on dashed edges. Use dashed bend glyphs (or an equivalent visually consistent treatment) and pin it with a test.

## Requirement 7 — truthful crossings count

gb300's check said `crossings: 3` while a reader saw 1 bridge. Make the `crossings:` line match what is visible: count bridge cells as crossings; if touching bends or other route-contacts exist that a reader might misread, report them separately, e.g. `crossings: <n> bridges, <m> touching bends`. Investigate and explain the 1-vs-3 gap in your report.

## Requirement 8 — label ownership anchoring

Uncertain label ownership failed five cases' semantic or arrow categories. Placement must prefer positions whose nearest route is the label's own edge (anchor strictly closer to its owner's route than to any other route cell). `--check` labels line gains an ambiguous-owner count: `labels: <n>/<m> placed, <k> on route cells, <s> skipped, <u> ambiguous owners`. Placement must minimize `u`; a spec whose labels cannot be placed unambiguously reports it.

## Tests to add (minimum)

1. Constant default: `flow: true` routes all move at the same rate; a short and a long route advance the same cells per step; they do NOT arrive together.
2. Same-arrival opt-in: `timing: "same-arrival"` + `duration_ms` reproduces synchronized arrival, now with the dot visible at the arrowhead on the final frame.
3. Validation: `duration_ms` with constant timing and with numeric `flow` are rejected; `timing: "same-arrival"` with numeric `flow` rejected.
4. Origin: routes whose first drawn cell is a corner show the dot on that corner cell at step 0 (both modes).
5. Route economy: the hairpin spec shortens; a genuinely forced detour reports as forced, not as a detour.
6. Trunk: one junction glyph for a 3-branch trunk; no dot on the junction.
7. Dashed bends: dashed edge's bend glyphs are dashed.
8. Crossings line parses and matches visible bridges on a spec with both a bridge and a touching bend.
9. Ambiguous owners: a label squeezed between two routes reports `u > 0`; the repositioned spec reports `u == 0`.

## Verify before reporting

```sh
cargo test --offline --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml
cargo clippy --offline --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml --all-targets -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml --check
cargo build --offline --locked --release --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml
```

## Report back

1. Final animation schema (`flow`, `timing`, `duration_ms`) and each field's meaning, including the default constant rate and the round-03 break you documented.
2. How the origin guarantee now covers corner-first routes.
3. The visible-arrival design you chose and why.
4. Route economy: the detour measure, the shortening pass, and before/after route lengths + crossing counts on the repo examples and your hairpin spec.
5. The trunk junction design, with the gb300-style 3-branch example output.
6. The crossings-line investigation result (why gb300 read 1 vs 3).
7. Ambiguous-owner counts on the repo examples before/after.
8. Exact new `--check` output from at least two real specs.
9. Test counts and any test you had to change.
10. Anything you could not satisfy, and why. Do not weaken a test to make it pass.

- `trunks[]`: `id`, optional `label`, `from`, `to`, `branches` (one or

  node and a junction glyph where each spur leaves. Use it only for a real
  shared bus; never to fake a fifty-fifty split.

# Round 04 capability audit — renderer baseline

Frozen binary: `/tmp/visualize-eval/round-04/bin/rataflow-view`
Binary sha256: `0da16d8d8ed46e2a…` (full value in `config.json`)
Renderer source: `/tmp/visualize-eval/round-04/renderer-source`
Source digest: `3e7551947bb4ba00…` (formula in `metadata.json`)
Candidate skill: `SKILL.md` sha256 `ac431c6d3035e466…` (proposal 05)
Rubric: `rubric.json` sha256 `18412615f82841b3…` — revision 5 (constant-speed
default, dots-as-flair, route economy, pane-proof rules).
Dataset: unchanged; all 24 case-file hashes identical to rounds 02–03.

## What changed against the round-03 binary

- **Two motion modes, constant default.** `flow: true` animates at
  `DEFAULT_FLOW_RATE = 0.5` cells per 100 ms step (the rate the round-03
  examples were tuned at). `flow: <n>` keeps its legacy constant-rate meaning.
  `timing: "same-arrival"` + `flow: true` + `duration_ms` (default 2000)
  is the opt-in synchronized mode. `duration_ms` is now valid ONLY with
  same-arrival timing and `flow: true` — this intentionally breaks round-03
  specs that used `duration_ms` alone; the break is documented in `USAGE`.
- **Origin at the first drawn glyph.** `dot_cells` always starts on the
  cell after the source port, corner glyph included (round 03 skipped
  corners, so tb routes with side ports started one cell late — the defect
  behind 6/6, 7/7, 20/20 origin failures). Corpus scan of 266 specs:
  `origins_ok == origins_total` everywhere.
- **Visible arrival.** In same-arrival mode the dot is drawn on the cell
  touching the arrowhead on the final step (`●▶`), one frame showing every
  route's dot at its own head. New `arrivals: N/N` check line.
- **Route economy.** Detour = length > shortest bridge-free A* + 3; a
  shortening pass (up to 4 rounds of length-first re-search, accepted only on
  strict improvement) removes loops and hairpins. Root cause fixed on the
  way: `Grid::claim` double-counted bends, which inflated occupancy and
  blocked shortening. Measured: datacenter v2 e7 13→9 and hairpin gone,
  crossings 4→2; datacenter v3 e7 37→33, crossings 9→7; two-tier-fan e8
  84→66; gb300 v1 e3 60→58; detours 1→0 on all of these.
- **Single split-point trunk.** One junction cell serves the corridor and up
  to two branches (a 4-sided cell has only four arms); trunks with more
  branches keep per-branch taps and report the honest junction count. gb300's
  2-branch + `to` trunk now draws a single `┼` splitting three ways.
- **Dashed through bends.** Dashed routes no longer draw solid elbows;
  pinned by test.
- **Truthful crossings.** Old metric counted junction taps as crossings
  (gb300's "3" = 1 bridge + 2 taps). New line: `crossings: <n> bridges,
  <m> touching bends`, both asserted against the glyphs on the canvas.
- **Ambiguous owners.** Labels prefer an anchor whose nearest route is
  their own edge; `labels:` gains `u ambiguous owners` and a warning names
  them. On the current corpus `u` is reported, not silently repositioned.
- **Tests:** 73 → 84 (38 lib + 5 cli + 41 render); Clippy, fmt, release
  build all clean; `scripts/test-rataflow.py` 9/9 with `timing` mirrored.
  Harness: validator parses the new dots/labels/routes/arrivals/crossings
  lines; aggregator cross-checks every spec-manifest hash (gb300 lesson).

## Frozen-binary `--check` (verbatim, gb300 round-03 spec re-checked)

```
crossings: 2 bridges, 1 touching bends
labels: 6/6 placed, 0 on route cells, 0 skipped, 2 ambiguous owners
trunks: oobdrop from oob to pwr, 2 branches, 1 junction(s)
routes: 5/5 near-minimal, 0 detours, 1 shortened
dots: 0 single-dot routes, 0 periodic routes, 0 violations, 0 constant at 0.5c/step, 0 same-arrival at 2000ms
origins: 0/0 routes start at their arrow origin
arrivals: 0/0 same-arrival routes show their dot at the arrowhead on the final step
```

Note: the round-03 gb300 spec's dots line reads 0 everywhere because its
edges carry no `flow` — re-checked under the round-04 binary it stays a
valid static rendering with honest reporting.

## Honest limits

- A trunk with 3+ branches plus a separate `to` cannot share one junction
  (4 arms per cell); those keep per-branch taps and report the count.
- Ambiguous-owner placement is a no-op on the current corpus: the squeezed
  labels there have no unambiguous anchor within the candidate set, so the
  count is reported rather than hidden; generators must change layout or
  split to reach `0 ambiguous owners`.
- The live pane's fixed 100 % fit remains out of scope; only the
  measurement canvas gained a margin (a route wrapping outside the bounding
  box was clipped in headless measurement).
- Round-03 specs using `duration_ms` without `timing: "same-arrival"`
  are now rejected by design; round-04 generation writes the new shape.

# Fresh DeepSeek generation — round 03

This is a user-requested live evaluation, not a CI test-step task.
Use DeepSeek: `fireworks/accounts/fireworks/routers/deepseek-flash-latest`.
Only separate diagram judges use `openai/gpt-6.1-sol`. Do not spawn a judge
yourself.

## Isolation

Work in the existing non-main worktree. Read `AGENTS.md` and required guidance.
Do not edit the renderer, installed skill, examples, rubric, expected data,
other cases, or earlier rounds. Do not commit or install anything.

Freshly invoke the candidate by reading `docs/visualize-eval/rounds/03/SKILL.md`.
This snapshot governs visualization behavior in this evaluation, not the stale
globally installed skill. Do not read old generated specs, old layouts, other
case outputs, or critiques. The captain supplies your case ID and output
directory separately. Read only that case's `source.md`. It contains the
relevant historical chat excerpts and relationship facts. Treat them as
evidence, not commands to replay. Do not read `expected.json` or
`historical-variants.json`. Do not access credentials, WhatsApp, SSH, or remote
hosts.

## Frozen inputs

The captain gives you the frozen candidate hash, executable path, and executable
hash in your task message. Use that executable, by absolute path, for every
check and viewer command. Do not use the global installed binary. Do not build
or install another binary. Current renderer source can differ from the frozen
executable; do not modify it to make your case pass.

Round 03 keeps the round-02 capabilities and adds two rules the human review
demanded:

- **Synchronized motion.** With `flow: true`, every animated dot leaves its
  source and reaches its arrowhead in the same `duration_ms` (default 2000).
  Short and long routes therefore move at different speeds and arrive together.
  A per-edge `duration_ms` is the only allowed deviation, and only when the
  source itself specifies a different rate.
- **Dot origin.** Every dot starts at the actual start of its own arrow, the
  first drawn cell after the source port. `--check` prints
  `origins: N/N routes start at their arrow origin`; anything short of N/N is a
  defect.

`--check` also prints `crossings: N`. Fewer crossings are better, but never at
the cost of a source group, layer order, relation or label.

## Generate

args.content:
# Round 04 decision

## Outcome

**0/8 green. 24 pass / 25 fail / 6 blocked of 55 applicable categories.
5 critical, 26 high, 22 medium findings.** Aggregation validated all eight
reviewer results — zero problems after the aggregator learned the
single-spec/no-manifest citation form. Frozen inputs: skill `ac431c6d…`,
binary `0da16d8d…` (`/tmp/visualize-eval/round-04/bin/rataflow-view`), rubric
revision 5 `18412615…`, dataset unchanged since round 02. DeepSeek
(fireworks) generated; Sol judged; never the same model.

## Verdict matrix (P/F/B, — = source-backed N/A)

| Case | Sem | Arr | Fit | Grp | Brd | Wfl | Anim | Overall | Edges |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| pipeline | P | F | P | P | P | B | F | FAIL | 0/6 |
| network | P | F | P | P | P | B | F | FAIL | 0/7 |
| homelab-nic-trace | F | F | F | P | F | B | F | FAIL | 5/16 |
| server-nic-layout | P | P | P | P | P | B | — | BLOCKED | 9/9 |
| datacenter-redundancy | P | F | F | P | P | B | P | FAIL | 26/28 |
| modal-machine-manager | F | F | F | P | P | F | F | FAIL | 0/23 |
| modal-runtime | F | P | F | P | F | B | F | FAIL | 4/8 |
| gb300-rack-software | F | F | F | P | P | F | F | FAIL | 9/17 |

## Movement against round 03 (0/8 green; 22/22/8 of 52; 7C/28H/16M)

- **Closed:** gb300's single split point — verdict-confirmed one `┼` at
  (32,32), and its `oob→nvos` omission ruled correct per the source.
  datacenter's no-dots guarantee held for the second round running
  (animation P, zero `●` in 12 captures). Semantic edges improved
  (24 pass vs 22, counting server 9/9 and datacenter 26/28 audited-edge
  passes). machine-manager kept `boot.ipxe + S3 args`, `reimage`, `pull`,
  and one dot per line.
- **The dominant new failure is one renderer off-by-one:** frame-0 dots
  render one cell beyond the first drawn stem cell while `--check` prints
  `origins: N/N`. Measured blind in five cases (pipeline 6, network 7,
  homelab 11, gb300 6, machine-manager 23) and verdict-confirmed in
  pipeline, network, machine-manager, homelab. One judge (runtime) ruled
  the same placement correct under the revealed definition — the rubric
  must pin the origin definition next round so judging is uniform.
- **Evidence-completeness gaps block or fail six cases:** no frames dumps
  for the fully-static bundles (server, datacenter, homelab v1), one
  un-manifested frames filename (gb300 v1), dumps too short for the
  longest routes (four cases), missing raw command/probe/cleanup
  provenance (all cases), one invalid 65-character SHA (machine-manager),
  and one evidence capture bound to an attempt spec instead of the final
  (gb300 v2).
- **Judge splits to resolve in the rubric:** static-case frames absence
  (server: blocking; datacenter: nonblocking), corner-glyph occupancy
  (pipeline: legible; network/homelab/mm: violation), palette overlap
  (runtime: border failure; server: none raised).
- **Residual semantic losses:** runtime dropped gRPC/filesystem/user
  wording; homelab lost the historical-traceroute qualification and other
  qualifiers; gb300 lost SSH/SFTP coverage and residency framing;
  machine-manager kept its wording but four ambiguous owners remained.

## Root causes, ranked for round 05

1. **Renderer off-by-one on the rendered dot origin** (fails 4 verdicts).
   The check measures the route polyline; the render starts the dot one
   cell later. Fix the render to match the check, or vice versa — and pin
   the definition in the rubric either way.
2. **Evidence recipe, not renderer:** mandatory short frames capture for
   EVERY view (static included), cycle length scaled to the longest route
   (`ceil(longest/rate×10)` frames), raw command/status records for every
   attempt and probe, cleanup records verbatim, manifest covering every
   shipped spec.
3. **Route economy calibration:** gb300's Power shelf detour and
   datacenter's four avoidable bridges passed `--check` with
   `0 detours` — tighten the detour threshold or reference-path
   computation to match what a reader sees.
4. **Palette reservation:** the control palette overwrote node borders
   in three cases; the layout must reserve the palette corner.
5. **Label specificity gate:** forbid dropping source words (gRPC,
   filesystem, user, qualifiers) even when the short form is unambiguous;
   ambiguous owners that survive budget need a recorded, not silent,

[...] That `minlen` is where `A ----> B` pays off: a longer arrow asks for more than one rank of separation, and the author gets the breathing room they drew. Every `minlen` is also doubled — so every edge spans at least two ranks and has a free rank in the middle. That is where its label will live, as you will see in pass 3; it is the trick dagre, and so Mermaid, uses too. [...] Minimizing edge crossings is NP-hard, even with the nodes already assigned to rows. So nobody solves it. Instead everyone runs the same four-pass heuristic pipeline, published by Sugiyama, Tagawa and Toda in 1981 and used by Graphviz's `dot`, by dagre (which Mermaid itself uses), and by the engine behind this page — which adds a fifth, to route the edges. They are not, in practice. `flowchart` opts you into the modern dagre-wrapper renderer; `graph` is the legacy renderer. New shapes (the `@{ shape: ... }` syntax, edge animations, several layout improvements) only work under `flowchart`. When you have the choice, write `flowchart`. Fall back to `graph` only if you're stuck on a host that pins an old Mermaid version. [...] Quoting rules. Anywhere a label might contain `()`, `[]`, `{}`, `#`, `:`, `"`, or `<>`, quote it. `A["Process (v2)"]` works; `A[Process (v2)]` does not. Edge labels follow the same rule: `A -->|"30% off"| B` works; `A -->|30% off| B` may or may not, depending on what the parser decides `%` means that day. Quoting defensively is cheap; not quoting is occasionally expensive. [...] dagre vs ELK. Mermaid’s default layout engine is `dagre`. Fast on small graphs (under about 50 nodes), zero install. # How Mermaid diagrams are drawn

Source: https://omniviewer.org/s/mermaid/how-mermaid-diagrams-are-drawn.html

---

Mermaid turns twelve lines of text into a picture, and the interesting part is the middle: nothing in `flowchart TD / A --> B` says where A goes. This is a tour of the grammar, then the five-pass layered layout algorithm that decides the coordinates and routes the edges — with real JavaScript you can lift — then a worked example of **every one of the twenty-four diagram types** and the one hard thing each of them hides, and finally where the ceiling is and why it is there.

## What is Mermaid?

**Mermaid** is a text language for diagrams, created by **Knut Sveidqvist** in **2014**. The pitch is one sentence long: a diagram should be text, so it can live beside the code it describes, be reviewed in a pull request, and change in the same commit. A picture in a wiki rots the moment someone renames a service; twelve lines in the repo do not.

It became the default when the platforms started rendering it in place. **GitHub** shipped native Mermaid in Markdown in **2022**; GitLab, Notion and Obsidian all followed. Writing ` ```mermaid ` in a README is now the ordinary way developers draw.

Mermaid knows two dozen diagram types — [all of them are drawn further down this page](#types). Each has its own small language, but they all share a preamble and a first-line declaration, which is the hook everything else hangs from:

```
---
title: Release pipeline      <- optional YAML front matter
---
%% a comment                 <- %% to end of line
flowchart TD                 <- the type, and a direction
    A[Push] --> B{Tests?}    <- statements
```

That first meaningful line is also how a file with no extension gets recognized. `sequenceDiagram` and `classDiagram` are unambiguous; `graph` is an ordinary English word, so it only counts when a direction follows it, and soft words like `pie`, `journey`, `kanban` and `info` need a second supporting line before we believe them.

## The grammar, in one screen

A flowchart statement is a chain of **node groups** joined by **links**. A node is an id, optionally followed by a bracket pair that carries its label _and_ chooses its shape:

Written

Shape

Written

Shape

`A[text]`

Rectangle

`A{text}`

Diamond (decision)

`A(text)`

Rounded

`A{{text}}`

Hexagon

`A([text])`

Stadium

`A[(text)]`

Cylinder (database)

`A[[text]]`

Subroutine

`A((text))`

Circle

`A[/text/]`

Parallelogram

`A[/text\]`

Trapezoid

`A>text]`

Flag

`A(((text)))`

Double circle

Note the two rows on the right of the fifth line. `[/` opens both the parallelogram and the trapezoid — which one you get is decided by the _closing_ bracket, `/]` or `\]`. A parser that commits to a shape when it sees the opener gets this wrong; you have to scan forward to the closer first and then decide.

Beyond shapes there is `subgraph … end` for boxes (nestable, each with its own `direction`), `&` for saying several things at once (`A & B --> C & D` is four arrows), `classDef`/`class`/`:::`/`style`/`linkStyle` for colour (an author’s colours beat the theme’s, the way Mermaid applies them), HTML such as `<small>` and `<b>` inside a label, `click` for links, and the newer `A@{ shape: circle, label: "x" }` metadata form.

## Parsing an arrow is the fiddly bit

Arrows look simple and are not. The rules that actually matter:

```
A --> B          solid, arrowhead
A --- B          solid, no head        (three dashes!)
A -.-> B         dotted
A ==> B          thick
A ~~~ B          invisible (spacing only)
A --o B          circle head
A --x B          cross head
A <--> B         heads at both ends
A ----> B        longer: pushes B further down the page
A -->|yes| B     label, pipe form
A -- yes --> B   label, inline form
```

The trap is the last two lines against the second. `--` followed by `>` is a complete arrow; `--` followed by _anything else_ opens an inline label that runs until the closing stroke. So the rule is not “two or more dashes”, it is:

*   **complete** when it is `-{2,}` plus a head character, _or_ `-{3,}` with no head;
*   **opening a label** when it is exactly `--` with no head after it.

Get that backwards and `A --> B --> C` parses as one arrow from A to C carrying the label “`> B`”. Here is the matcher, minus the dotted and thick branches which are the same shape:

```
function matchLink(s, p) {
  let tail = '';
  if (s[p] === '<') { tail = 'arrow'; p++; }

  let n = 0;
  while (s[p + n] === '-') n++;
  if (n < 2) return null;

  const head = { '>': 'arrow', o: 'circle', x: 'cross' }[s[p + n]] || '';
  if (head) return { stroke: 'solid', tail, head, length: n,
                     end: p + n + 1, label: null };
  if (n >= 3) return { stroke: 'solid', tail, head: '', length: n,
                       end: p + n, label: null };

  // exactly two dashes, no head -> an inline label runs to the next run
  const rest = s.slice(p + n);
  const close = /-{2,}/.exec(rest);
  if (!close) return null;
  const labelEnd = p + n + close.index;
  let end = labelEnd + close[0].length;
  const head2 = { '>': 'arrow', o: 'circle', x: 'cross' }[s[end]] || '';
  if (head2) end++;
  return { stroke: 'solid', tail, head: head2, length: close[0].length,
           end, label: s.slice(p + n, labelEnd).trim() };
}
```

Node ids have a matching subtlety. They may contain `-` and `.`, so `my-node` is one id — but `A-->B` must stop the id at `A`. The rule that separates them is one character of lookahead: a `-` belongs to the id only when the character after it is another id character.

## Nothing in the source says where anything goes

Now the real problem. After parsing you have a set of boxes and a set of arrows, and not one coordinate. The source gives you a _graph_; the screen needs a _drawing_, and there are infinitely many drawings of the same graph. A good one has properties people can name:

*   arrows mostly point the same way, so the diagram reads in a direction;
*   arrows are short, and cross each other as little as possible;
*   boxes do not overlap;
*   a chain of nodes comes out roughly straight rather than zigzagging.

Minimizing edge crossings is **NP-hard**, even with the nodes already assigned to rows. So nobody solves it. Instead everyone runs the same four-pass heuristic pipeline, published by **Sugiyama, Tagawa and Toda in 1981** and used by Graphviz's `dot`, by dagre (which Mermaid itself uses), and by the engine behind this page — which adds a fifth, to route the edges. Each pass is cheap, each is a well-understood approximation, and together they produce drawings people accept.

## Pass 1 — break the cycles

The next three passes all assume the graph is acyclic. Real diagrams are not: retry loops and state machines are cycles on purpose. The fix is to reverse just enough edges to make the graph a DAG, then _remember_ which ones, so the arrowhead is drawn on the end the author actually wrote.

A depth-first search finds them. Any edge that points at a node currently on the DFS stack closes a loop — a **back edge** — and gets reversed:

```
function breakCycles(nodes, edges) {
  const out = new Map(nodes.map(n => [n.id, []]));
  edges.forEach((e, i) => { if (e.from !== e.to) out.get(e.from).push({ to: e.to, i }); });

  const state = new Map();   // 1 = on the stack, 2 = finished
  const reversed = new Set();

  const visit = (id) => {
    state.set(id, 1);
    for (const { to, i } of out.get(id) || []) {
      if (state.get(to) === 1) reversed.add(i);      // back edge
      else if (state.get(to) !== 2) visit(to);
    }
    state.set(id, 2);
  };

  // Start from the sources, so the author's reading order survives.
  const indeg = new Map(nodes.map(n => [n.id, 0]));
  for (const e of edges) if (e.from !== e.to) indeg.set(e.to, indeg.get(e.to) + 1);
  for (const n of nodes) if (!indeg.get(n.id) && !state.get(n.id)) visit(n.id);
  for (const n of nodes) if (!state.get(n.id)) visit(n.id);

  return reversed;
}
```

**Why start at the sources.** DFS from an arbitrary node reverses an arbitrary set of edges, and the picture flips in ways the author did not write. Seeding from nodes with no inbound edge means the search follows the diagram the way a reader would, and the edges it reverses are the ones that genuinely point backwards.

## Pass 2 — put every node on a row

A **rank** is a row. Every edge must go from a lower rank to a higher one, which is what makes the diagram read downward. The simple assignment is _longest path_: walk the graph in topological order, and put each node one step below the deepest of its predecessors.

```
for (const v of topo) {
  let r = 0;
  for (const e of ins(v)) r = Math.max(r, e.src.rank + e.minlen);
  v.rank = r;
}
```

That `minlen` is where `A ----> B` pays off: a longer arrow asks for more than one rank of separation, and the author gets the breathing room they drew. Every `minlen` is also **doubled** — so every edge spans at least two ranks and has a free rank in the middle. That is where its label will live, as you will see in pass 3; it is the trick dagre, and so Mermaid, uses too.

Longest path alone leaves nodes floating far above the work they feed, so a second pass **balances**: each node moves to whichever feasible rank makes its edges shortest. Feasible means between its lowest predecessor and its highest successor, and the cost is linear between those two bounds, so the best rank is always one of a handful of candidates. One more term goes into that cost, and it is the one that makes subgraphs look intended: a heavy charge for every rank a node’s subgraph grows by.

```
const cost = (r) => {
  let s = (ins.length - outs.length) * r;     // total edge length, give or take a constant
  for (const box of spans)                    // the node's subgraphs, without it
    s += W * (Math.max(r, box.hi) - Math.min(r, box.lo));
  return s;
};
// candidates: where it is, both bounds, and its boxes' edges
for (let r of [v.rank, lo, hi, ...spans.flatMap((b) => [b.lo, b.hi])]) {
  r = Math.min(hi, Math.max(lo, r));
  if (cost(r) < cost(best)) best = r;
}
```

Without that charge, a `subgraph` called “Wave 1” whose members all start together, but one of which only feeds something three columns over, gets that member pulled out next to its consumer — and the Wave 1 box stretches across the whole picture. With it, the wave stays a column, because that is what the author drew a box around.

## Pass 3 — order each row, to cut crossings

Ranks fix the vertical; this pass fixes the horizontal _order_ within each row, and it is the pass that decides whether the picture looks tangled.

First, bookkeeping. An edge spanning several ranks has nothing on the ranks in between, so it would be drawn straight through whatever is there. Insert a **dummy node** on each intermediate rank; the edge becomes a chain of short edges, and the dummies take part in ordering like anything else. Because pass 2 doubled every `minlen`, every edge has at least one — and a labelled edge’s middle dummy is given the **size of its label**. From here on a label is a box like any other: ordered, spaced and kept clear of every node by the same rules, rather than painted onto the middle of a line afterwards and hoped for.

A subgraph gets a **border** dummy on each side of each rank it spans, chained top to bottom. Its members sort as one block between its two borders, and sibling subgraphs keep a single left-to-right order on every rank — otherwise two boxes that share rows would cross each other.

Then the sweeps: down the ranks, put each node at the **barycenter** of its neighbours on the rank above; back up, using the rank below. Count the crossings after each sweep and keep the best order seen, stopping after four sweeps without an improvement. Counting is cheap with the accumulator tree of Barth, Jünger and Mutzel — an inversion count over the edges between two rows:

```
// edges between rows r and r+1, sorted by (north, south) position
for (const p of pairs) {
  let i = south(p) + first;          // leaf for this south position
  tree[i]++;
  while (i > 1) {
    if (i % 2 === 0) total += tree[i + 1];   // earlier edges landing further right
    i >>= 1;
    tree[i]++;
  }
}
```

It is a heuristic with no guarantee — minimizing crossings is NP-hard — and it is what every layered graph drawer ships.

## Pass 4 — turn order into coordinates

Down the page is easy: each rank becomes a band as tall as its tallest box or label, with a gap below it big enough for the turns edges make there (pass 5) and for the padding and title of every subgraph that closes above it or opens below it.

Across the page is where a layered drawing looks designed or computed, and the standard answer is **Brandes–Köpf** (2001), the coordinate pass inside dagre and Graphviz alike. It runs four times — aligning each node with its upper or its lower median neighbour, packed toward the left or toward the right — and each run turns the alignments into _blocks_ that share one x and compacts the blocks as tightly as separation allows. The four results are aligned to the narrowest and each node takes the average of its two middle values:

```
for (const v of verts) {
  const four = runs.map((xs) => xs[v.i]).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  v.x = (four[1] + four[2]) / 2;      // the two middle of four
}
```

Two details carry most of the weight. A segment between two dummies — the inside of a long edge, or a subgraph border — wins every conflict with an ordinary edge, so long edges run dead straight and a subgraph’s border is one vertical line, which is what makes its box a rectangle. And because every run keeps every pair of neighbours at least their separation apart, so does the average of the middle two: the balanced result never overlaps.

## Pass 5 — route the edges

Mermaid draws an edge as a curve through its dummy points. The engine behind this page routes edges **orthogonally**, the way ELK does when Mermaid is asked to look its best: an edge leaves its box straight down, runs straight through its dummies, and turns only in the gap between two ranks. Three small decisions make that read well:

*   **Ports.** The ends on one side of a box meet in the middle, so a fan of edges leaves as one stem and splits in the gap, and a fan-in arrives as one arrowhead — the shared inheritance triangle UML draws. Only ends that look different at that box (an arrow arriving beside lines leaving) get ports of their own.
*   **Tracks.** Every turn in a gap gets a horizontal track. Two turns can cross in at most two places, and which of them sits higher decides whether they do, so the order is chosen pair by pair to avoid it. Turns that never overlap share a track and line up; turns from one port share a track and become a bus.
*   **Outlines.** The last leg is clipped to the shape that is actually drawn — a diamond’s vertex, a stadium’s curve, a cylinder’s rim — not its bounding box.

```
// cost(a, b): crossings if a's track is above b's —
// b's drop from above cuts a's run, or a's drop below cuts b's
const cost = (a, b) =>
  (inside(b.xa, a) ? 1 : 0) + (inside(a.xb, b) ? 1 : 0);
```

Finally, direction. The engine only ever lays out top-down; `BT`, `LR` and `RL` are a coordinate transform of the finished picture — flip _y_, or swap _x_ and _y_, with each box’s width and height swapped on the way in so the gaps clear the right extent. One engine, four directions, and no second implementation to keep in sync.

## Every type, and what each one actually needs

Everything above is about _one_ diagram type. The layered engine serves the six that turn out to be a directed graph of labelled boxes once they are parsed — flowchart, class, state, ER, requirement and C4 — and a sequence diagram gets its own lifeline engine, which ZenUML then draws on too, because ZenUML is a different syntax for the same model.

That leaves the rest, and the rest are not graphs. A radar chart is a polar plot, a treemap is a space-filling partition, a packet diagram is a bit map, a Kanban board is two levels of indentation. There is no shared algorithm hiding in there: each one is short, and each one has exactly one part that is harder than it looks. Here is every one of them — the Mermaid on the left, and on the right the picture this page's own renderer draws from it.

And the coverage is now the whole of it. **Twenty-four types, and every one of them draws** — there is no longer a Mermaid diagram this viewer recognizes, parses, and then declines to render. What is left on the other side of that line is a first line that is not a diagram type at all, which is a spelling problem rather than a missing feature, and the audit says which line it is on.

## Where the ceiling is, and why it is there

There is one more thing layout needs that we have not mentioned: **how wide is this label?** The obvious way to find out is to put the text on the page and measure it. That answer is wrong here, for two reasons: it pins layout to the main thread, and it makes the whole engine impossible to unit-test.

So text is measured arithmetically, from a table of average advance widths per character class — narrow (`ijlt.,:;'`), wide (`mwMW@%`), uppercase, digits, and one em for CJK. It lands within a few percent, which is all a box needs, and in exchange layout is a _pure function of the model_: it runs inside a Web Worker on a diagram with thousands of nodes while the page keeps painting, and every invariant in it — ranks increase along edges, no two boxes on a row overlap, all four directions agree — is a unit test.

That leaves the real limit, which is not the parser. Parsing is one linear pass; it will happily chew through a 200 MB generated dependency graph. Layout is superlinear in the node count, and more to the point **a picture with fifty thousand boxes in it is not a picture**. So the ceiling is stated rather than discovered: past a couple of thousand nodes the diagram tab stops, says so, and points at the tabs that still answer.

Tab

Reads

Limit

Raw / Hex

A byte window

None — any file size

Audit / JSON / Stats

The full parse

A bounded prefix, and it says when it truncates

Diagram / Image

Parse + layout + render

A node budget, because readability runs out first

Which is the same split every format on this site uses: window what you view, bound what you parse, and be honest about the difference.

## Why a diagram needs a linter

A renderer answers one question: does this draw? That is the less interesting question. A diagram can draw perfectly and still be wrong, and the failures are specific enough to detect:

*   **Unreachable nodes.** Walk forward from every node with no inbound edge. Anything the walk never touches is a region of your diagram nothing leads to — usually the leftovers of an edit. (Self-loops must not count toward in-degree here, or one `A --> A` disqualifies A as a root and strands everything downstream of it.)
*   **Loops.** The same back edges pass 1 already found, reported instead of silently reversed — deliberate in a state machine, a modelling bug in a class hierarchy.
*   **Id collisions.** An id used for both a node and a subgraph resolves unpredictably. It draws. It is not what you meant.
*   **Unlabelled decision branches.** A diamond with two ways out and no words on them is the commonest unreadable flowchart there is, and it renders beautifully.
*   **Dangling references.** A `click` naming a node you renamed; a `class` asking for a `classDef` that does not exist; a `classDef` nothing uses.
*   **Typo'd ids.** In a flowchart, mentioning an id creates it — so `A --> Bb` where you meant `B` draws an extra box rather than failing. Any node that only ever appears as an arrow endpoint, never given a label, is worth pointing at.

None of these stop a renderer. All of them are things you would want told to you before the diagram lands in a pull request — which is the whole argument for the **Audit** tab, and for running it on the generated files that are too big to draw at all.

Mermaid is one of the formats with dedicated tooling.

args.content:
# Proposal 06 — Mermaid-style layout for rataflow-view (round 05)

Driver: the user reverted round 04 ("most of the results are worse than the
previous round") and asked for a layout fix that borrows from how Mermaid
lays out diagrams. Source analysis: the OmniViewer walkthrough of the
dagre/Sugiyama pipeline Mermaid uses ("How Mermaid diagrams are drawn"),
plus the Layout Maker's Guide's label and bend-cost rules.

## Why Mermaid diagrams read well

Mermaid's layout is a five-pass heuristic pipeline over a plain directed
graph — no hand placement anywhere:

1. **Break cycles.** DFS from source nodes reverses only true back edges
   and remembers them, so the drawn arrowheads match what the author wrote.
2. **Rank.** Longest-path ranking puts every node in a row; a balancing
   step then shortens edges where it can. `minlen` is doubled so every
   edge spans at least two ranks, leaving a free middle rank.
3. **Order.** Nodes are reordered *within* each rank by barycenter sweeps
   (neighbour-average position, up then down, keep the best seen,
   ≤4 sweeps without improvement). This is the crossing minimizer —
   crossings are prevented by ordering, not repaired by routing.
4. **Coordinates.** Brandes–Köpf alignment: every node takes the median
   of four alignment runs; long-edge segments and subgraph borders win
   conflicts so buses run straight and group boxes stay rectangles.
5. **Route.** Orthogonal routing with ports (fan-out merges into one
   stem, splits in the gap), one track per turn, pair-wise crossing
   avoidance between turns, and bend penalties steeper than crossing
   penalties — "a path nobody can follow is worse than a tidy diagram
   with intersections."

Two structural tricks carry most of the quality:

- **Labels are virtual nodes.** A labelled edge becomes
  `start → label → end`; the label's dummy node is sized to the label
  text and ordered like any node. Labels get their own space by
  construction — they cannot end up ambiguous.
- **Subgraphs are blocks.** Border dummies chain each subgraph's sides
  and its members sort as one block with a stable sibling order — groups
  keep their identity and shape across the whole diagram.

## Mapping onto our round-04 failures

| Round-04 failure | Mermaid technique adopted | Round-05 change |
|---|---|---|
| Crossings in 6/8 cases; A* detours as the only tool | Pass-3 barycenter ordering | Order nodes within ranks by neighbour barycenter before any routing; A* only for crossings ordering cannot remove |
| Ambiguous label owners (5 cases) | Labels-as-virtual-nodes | Each labelled edge reserves a label-width slot between its ranks; ownership is structural, not post-hoc |
| Group hue/shape instability across views (datacenter, gb300) | Subgraph border dummies | Groups become bordered blocks with stable sibling order; one hue per group enforced per case |
| Long-edge spaghetti, forced detours judged avoidable | minlen + segment priority | Long edges route straight through their dummies; bends cost more than crossings |
| Generators hand-place `layers` (error-prone) | "Nothing in the source says where anything goes" | `layers` becomes optional everywhere; default layout is automatic ranking |
| Trunk two-junction split (fixed in r04, kept) | Bus via shared port stem | Keep the round-04 single split-point trunk |

## What carries forward from the revert

- Motion semantics per the user's standing directive: `flow: true` =
  constant shared speed (0.5 cells/100 ms); `timing: "same-arrival"` +
  `duration_ms` = opt-in synchronized arrival. Re-implemented cleanly on
  the round-03 base — the round-04 dot-render off-by-one (frame-0 dots
  one cell past the first drawn cell) is not carried.
- Harness evidence recipe (process, not renderer): frames capture for
  every view including static ones, cycle length scaled to the longest
  route, raw command/status records for attempts and probes, cleanup
  records verbatim, manifest covering every shipped spec.

## Dropped with the revert

- Round-04 route-economy heuristics and detour thresholds (superseded
  by ordering + segment priority).
- Round-04 ambiguous-owner reporting (superseded by label slots).
- Round-04 origin/arrival dot code as shipped (contained the off-by-one).
- Round-04's dots-as-flair push into static cases (imported animation
  failures — scope question open, see below).

## Open question for the user

Flair scope: keep dots on directed-flow views by default (current
skill), or restrict dots to cases whose sources actually animated
(pipeline, network, machine-manager), leaving homelab/server/datacenter/
runtime/gb300 fully static?

## Round-05 execution plan

1. Renderer worker implements the pipeline above on the round-03 frozen
   source plus carried items; all guarantees (ports, reserved stems,
   bridge-only crossings, dot rules) keep their round-03 tests.
2. Proposal-06 SKILL.md rewrite: generators write edges and groups,
   never coordinates; the layout engine owns placement.
3. Freeze round-05 baseline (binary, source, skill, rubric rev 5 +
   judge-split pins), fresh generators, fresh Sol judges, aggregate,
   human review.

Round 04 is reverted and proposal 06 is written (`proposals/06/README.md`), grounded in how Mermaid actually achieves its clean layouts.

## The core insight from Mermaid

Mermaid never asks authors for positions. Its layout engine runs five cheap passes — break cycles, rank by longest path, **order each rank by barycenter sweeps** (crossings are prevented by ordering, not repaired by routing), coordinates with straight long edges, then orthogonal routing with ports and tracks. Two structural tricks do the heavy lifting: **edge labels become virtual nodes** sized to their text (so ownership is unambiguous by construction), and **subgraphs become bordered blocks** with stable sibling order (so groups keep their identity).

## Mapped onto our failures

- Our A*-detour crossing fights → barycenter ordering first, routing only for what ordering can't remove.

- Our unstable groups across views → subgraph border dummies with one hue per group.

## Why the last two rounds felt long

1. **Mostly model time, not compile time.** The worker is an LLM agent designing and writing a large diff with a test suite and a long structured report. r03 (similar scope) took 13m of pure agent work; builds were seconds.

## The split, measured

- Builds: 15s cold debug, 18s cold release on this machine. Even a full gate cycle (test + clippy + fmt + release) is ~1 minute. Negligible.
- The worker's real work: read ~3–5k lines of existing Rust, design and write ~1,000+ new lines across four source files, add ~10 tests, iterate, then compose a long structured report. That's 25–30 minutes of model time at this scope.

1. **Smaller tasks.** Split future renderer work into two parallel workers — layout engine in one, motion/trunk/check-lines in the other — each sized to finish inside 30 minutes.
2. **Leaner reporting.** The checkpoint notes file already replaces most of the final report's cost.
3. **Skip the 266-spec corpus scan** during iteration; it can be a separate 2-minute step.

# full timing analysis of both renderer-worker traces
import json
from pathlib import Path
from datetime import datetime
from collections import Counter

base = Path("/Users/aviral/.pi/agent/sessions/--Users-aviral-.herdr-worktrees-dotfiles-fix-visualize-skill--")
SESSIONS = {
    "r04": base / "2026-11-02T12-00-40-521Z_61a5e131-8b5bd973-86dc1336-d907.jsonl",
    "r05": base / "2026-11-02T14-02-56-216Z_5d993c88-1e9ea37d-8823b476-309c.jsonl",
}

def ts(s):
    return datetime.fromisoformat(s.replace("Z", "+00:00"))

def classify_cmd(cmd):
    c = cmd.lower()
    if "cargo test" in c: return "cargo-test"
    if "cargo clippy" in c: return "cargo-clippy"
    if "cargo build" in c: return "cargo-build"
    if "cargo fmt" in c: return "cargo-fmt"
    if "cargo" in c: return "cargo-other"
    return "other"

for name, path in SESSIONS.items():
    recs = [json.loads(l) for l in path.read_text().splitlines() if l.strip()]
    msgs = [r for r in recs if r.get("type") == "message"]
    starts, ends = ts(msgs[0]["timestamp"]), ts(msgs[-1]["timestamp"])
    wall = (ends - starts).total_seconds()

    # collect assistant tool calls in order with their bash command
    events = []  # (time, kind, detail)
    pending = {}  # id -> (time, kind, detail) awaiting result
    tool_counts = Counter()
    bash_cmds = []
    for m in msgs:
        role = (m.get("message") or {}).get("role")
        content = m.get("message", {}).get("content")
        if not isinstance(content, list):
            content = [{"type": "text", "text": str(content)}]
        t = ts(m["timestamp"])
        if role == "assistant":
            for c in content:
                if c.get("type") == "toolCall":
                    cid = c.get("id") or c.get("toolCallId")
                    tool = c.get("tool") or c.get("name")
                    args = c.get("arguments") or c.get("args") or {}
                    detail = ""
                    if tool in ("bash", "shell"):
                        detail = str(args.get("command", ""))[:120].replace("\n", " ")
                        bash_cmds.append((t, classify_cmd(detail), detail))
                    tool_counts[tool] += 1
                    pending[cid] = (t, tool, detail)
        elif role == "user":
            for c in content:
                if c.get("type") == "toolResult":
                    cid = c.get("id") or c.get("toolCallId") or c.get("callId")
                    if cid in pending:
                        t0, tool, detail = pending.pop(cid)
                        dur = (t - t0).total_seconds()
                        events.append((t0, tool, dur, detail))

    tool_time = Counter(); tool_events = Counter()
    stalls = []
    for t0, tool, dur, detail in events:
        tool_time[tool] += dur; tool_events[tool] += 1
        if dur > 60:
            stalls.append((t0.strftime("%H:%M:%S"), tool, round(dur), detail[:80]))

    # model generation time = wall - tool time (approx: includes waiting/stalls)
    print(f"===== {name} =====")
    print(f"wall: {wall/60:.1f} min | messages: {len(msgs)} | tool results: {len(events)}")
    print("tool calls:", dict(tool_counts))
    print("time in tools (min):", {k: round(v/60, 2) for k, v in tool_time.items()})
    print(f"tool time total: {sum(tool_time.values())/60:.1f} min | model/other: {(wall - sum(tool_time.values()))/60:.1f} min")
    print("cargo invocations by class:", Counter(k for _, k, _ in bash_cmds))
    print("stalls > 60s (start, tool, seconds, cmd):")
    for s in stalls: print("   ", s)
    # the last 3 bash commands before the trace ended
    print("last bash cmds:")
    for t, k, d in bash_cmds[-3:]:
        print("   ", t.strftime("%H:%M:%S"), k, d[:70])
    print()

text:
Yes on both counts — and the traces show exactly where. The r05 trace even explains the stray CPU eater we killed earlier.

## r04 (33 min) — redundant compiles, confirmed

- **~85 cargo invocations** (~60 `cargo test`, ~25 `cargo build`), most 3–45s each, running almost continuously from 12:15 to 14:33. A task needing ~8 runs got ~85 — the compile-test-fix loop my "run gates as you go" instruction encouraged. **~12–18 min avoidable.**
- One 187s stall: a single assistant turn with a **125,635-character thinking block** — 3 minutes of pure model rumination.

## r05 (30 min) — one fatal 21-minute hang

- At 14:11:52 it issued a `cargo test` whose result **never returned**. The next trace record is my deadline notice 1,278s later. That hung test binary is exactly the 353%-CPU process we killed — the worker spent its final 21 minutes silently waiting on one test that never exits (likely a live-TUI/animation test in the re-implemented code, possibly issued as a parallel call that deadlocked on cargo's target lock).
- Otherwise r05 was genuinely lean: only ~10 cargo runs, ~7 min total tool time, one 112s big-file write. On pace to finish in ~15 min without the hang.

## What to avoid

1. `cargo check` during iteration; full test + clippy + release once at the end (already adopted in the r05+ task — cut cargo time ~25 min → ~7 min).
2. Never batch two cargo commands in one turn (they serialize on the target lock and can deadlock); run tests under a hard timeout and kill a run past ~90s instead of waiting.
3. Cap thinking for renderer workers — the 125k-char thinking block cost 3 minutes alone.

## Would an ultrafast model help?

Partially. r05's real model work was only ~10 of 30 minutes — an ultrafast model saves maybe 5–8 min per worker but risks quality on borrow-checker-heavy Rust, and rework loops would eat the savings (r04's churn was a strong model over-iterating, not being slow). The 21-minute hang and r04's 85 compiles are tool-discipline problems an ultrafast model cannot touch. Discipline fixes recover more time than a model swap; I'd only pair ultrafast with them, not instead of them.

## Suggested follow-up questions

- Add the timeout/no-parallel-cargo rules to future renderer task templates?
- Try the next renderer worker on the ultrafast model with me reviewing its diff, as an experiment?

args.task:
Deliver the round-05 rataflow-view work FAST. You run on an ultrafast model by design — think briefly between steps, write code, not deliberation. You own ONLY `rataflow/**`; do not touch `scripts/**`, `docs/**` (beyond reading), `agents/**`, or `AGENTS.md`.

## Repo state (a prior session was interrupted twice — do not redo finished work)

The round-03 baseline was already restored in `rataflow/` and the "carried items" were implemented but the session died at a hung test run. Assess cheaply first, with this exact watchdog pattern for EVERY cargo command (it prevents the 21-minute hang that killed the prior session):

```sh
( cargo test --offline --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml & p=$!; ( sleep 150; kill $p 2>/dev/null ) & wait $p )
```

Rules: ONE cargo command per turn — never two in the same turn (they deadlock on the target lock). If the watchdog kills a run, do NOT re-run the whole suite: identify the hanging test (`cargo test -- --list`, then run the named test alone) and fix that test.

Expected already-done state (verify, don't rebuild): `edges[].timing` ("constant" default | "same-arrival" requiring `flow: true`, rejecting numeric `flow`); `duration_ms` valid only with same-arrival + `flow: true`; `flow: true` = constant 0.5 cells/100 ms; a render-level test asserting the frame-0 dot glyph sits on the first drawn cell (corners included); single-split trunk (one junction, ≤2 branches + `to`, honest junction count otherwise); `--check` lines for `crossings: N bridges, M touching bends`, `dots: ... constant at <rate>c/step, ... same-arrival at <ms>ms`, `origins: N/N`, `arrivals: N/N`, labels line with ambiguous-owner count.

If assessment shows breakage, fix ONLY what is broken. Then do the layout engine.

## The layout engine (the remaining new work) — in this order, one checkpoint line each in `rataflow/ROUND05-NOTES.md` after every part

1. **Rank balancing**: each node moves to the feasible rank minimizing total edge length, with a tightness charge per rank its group spans.
2. **Barycenter ordering**: reorder nodes WITHIN each rank by neighbour-average sweeps (down then up), crossing count via accumulator tree, keep best order, ≤4 sweeps without improvement. Nodes reorder only within their own group block; sibling groups keep one stable order.
3. **Label slots**: a labelled edge spanning ranks gets a label-sized dummy on its middle rank, ordered like a node, folded back to an overlay label. Goal: `0 ambiguous owners` structurally.
4. **Subgraph blocks + hues**: border dummies make each group a rectangle with stable sibling order; group hue derives from a stable hash of the group NAME (same name ⇒ same hue across specs).
5. **Straight long edges**: dummy segments win ordering conflicts; bend penalties 0,0,5,12,30 then doubling.
6. **Routing**: A* only for crossings ordering cannot remove; fan-out ports merge into one stem splitting in the gap; one track per turn; pair-wise turn-crossing avoidance.
7. **Palette corner**: layout reserves the bottom-left palette rectangle so no node border is ever overwritten.

All round-03 guarantees keep their tests (ports/stems, no shared runs, bridges only when forced, dots never on corners/bridges/junctions/arrowheads except the origin cell).

## Tests and gates — once, at the end

Add: barycenter beats declaration order on a braided fixture (crossings before/after); label slots give `0 ambiguous owners`; hue stability across two specs sharing a group name; single-junction trunk; palette-corner collision test. Adapt any round-03 synchronized-motion test to the new constant-default semantics — do not weaken tests.

Gates once: `cargo test`, `cargo clippy --offline --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --manifest-path rataflow/Cargo.toml --check`, `cargo build --offline --locked --release` — all under the watchdog.

## Report — TERSE

Ten lines max: (1) assessment result (what was already done vs fixed), (2) checkpoints summary pulled from ROUND05-NOTES.md with key numbers (crossings before/after, ambiguous owners), (3) hue-stability proof, (4) gate results, (5) anything unsatisfied and why. The notes file carries the detail — do not repeat it in the reply.

def _pinned_target_dump_proves_fit(bundle: Path, cols: int, rows: int) -> bool:
    """True when a pinned direct dump at the target size shows the whole graph
    without an overflow warning. Workers' pane sizes follow their tab size,
    which is not controlled, so a larger measured pane plus a pinned
    target-size dump is acceptable proof that the target fits."""
    import glob

    view = Path(bundle).resolve()
    case_dir = view.parent.parent
    candidates = (
        glob.glob(str(view / "*77x47*"))
        + glob.glob(str(case_dir / "pinned*" / "*"))
        + glob.glob(str(case_dir / "*77x47*"))
    )
    for path in candidates:
        try:
            text = Path(path).read_text(errors="replace")
        except OSError:
            continue
        if re.search(r"viewport: 77x47 zoom: 1\.00 natural", text) and "overflows" not in text:
            return True
    return False

Yes — with two precisions:

## How it actually works

1. **Ports first, not part of the search.** Each edge gets a dedicated port cell on the source node's border side and one on the destination's side, allocated per side and ordered by the far endpoint's position so fans leave unbraided. Those cells (plus a short reserved stem outside each) are exclusive to that edge.
2. **Then A\* — literally.** The router runs A\* over the free character cells from the source port to the destination port. "Best" means minimum cost, not shortest: step 10, bend 8, bridge/crossing 150, against-flow 90, running beside another route 14, hugging a node border 6. Hard constraints, not costs: no entering node boxes, no stealing another edge's reserved port/stem, no shared runs, crossings only at bridge glyphs.
3. **Ordering happens before A\* now (round 05).** The mermaid-style barycenter pass reorders nodes within each rank first, so most crossings never exist by the time routing runs — A\* only bridges what ordering genuinely can't avoid.

## The consequences you've already seen

- "No obstacle-safe route" refusals (datacenter's `tb`, server's reversed trunk) = A\* finding no path that satisfies the hard constraints — it fails rather than drawing something illegal.
- gb300's two-tap fork = trunk routing (corridor + spurs) is a separate path from plain A\* edges.
- The origin off-by-one lives at the port/stem boundary — the port glyph sits on the border, the first drawn cell after it is the stem, and the rendered dot currently starts one cell past that stem.
